title: Rebase Beyond the Basics: autosquash, --onto, and Staying Current
intro: Rebase replays your commits on top of another base, producing new commits. Used on your own unpushed work it gives reviewers a clean story. Used on shared history it rewrites what other people have built on. The CI/CD category introduced rebase; this covers the forms that solve real problems.

steps.prompt: Your branch has fixup! commits from earlier (git-tutorial-002). Squash each into its target commit automatically while rebasing onto main.
steps.fake_output:
pick a1b2c3d Validate currency before charging
fixup 9e8d7c6 fixup! Validate currency before charging
pick 5d6e7f8 Charge in cents, not dollars

Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/fix/charge-cents.
steps.explanation: The fixup commit was moved under its target and squashed in; the branch now has two clean commits.
steps.why: --autosquash reads the 'fixup!' prefixes and arranges the todo list for you. Set 'rebase.autoSquash true' and it happens on every interactive rebase.

steps.prompt: You branched feature/reports off feature/auth by mistake, and auth isn't ready. Move just your reports commits so they sit on main instead.
steps.explanation: The commits that are on feature/reports but not on feature/auth were replayed onto main.
steps.why: Read '--onto A B C' as: take the commits in C that aren't in B, and put them on A. It's the tool for 'I branched from the wrong place' and for removing a range of commits from the middle of a branch. A plain 'git rebase main' would have dragged the unfinished auth commits along.

steps.prompt: A rebase stops on a conflict. After resolving and staging the file, carry on.
steps.fake_output:
[detached HEAD 2c3d4e5] Add monthly report endpoint
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/reports.
steps.why: A rebase applies commits one at a time, so you may resolve conflicts several times, once per commit. If it goes wrong, 'git rebase --abort' restores the branch exactly as it was, and even after finishing, 'git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD' undoes the whole rebase.

steps.prompt: Update your branch with new commits from the remote by rebasing your local commits on top, instead of creating a merge commit.
steps.explanation: Your local commits now sit on top of the latest remote ones: a straight line of history.
steps.why: Plain 'git pull' merges, which scatters 'Merge branch main of ...' commits through a branch. 'pull --rebase' keeps it linear. Many teams set 'pull.rebase true' globally.

steps.prompt: You rebased a branch you had already pushed. Push it without overwriting anything a teammate may have pushed since you last fetched.
steps.explanation: The remote branch now matches your rebased one.
steps.why: A rebased branch needs a force push, because its commits have new ids. --force-with-lease refuses if the remote moved since your last fetch, so you can't silently destroy someone else's commits; plain --force would. Never rebase main or any branch other people build on.
